title: Nothing at random
hook: let no act be done without a purpose (Meditations 4.2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: fire eats obstacles. Your line was fuel. What blocked you, and what did it become fuel for? Day five hundred fifty-one.

You pick up your phone. Thirty seconds later you're looking at a stranger's kitchen renovation, and you can't remember why you picked it up. You walk into a room and stand there. You open the fridge and close it. Much of an ordinary day happens on its own, like a car that drives itself while you're thinking about something else. Marcus Aurelius wrote one of the shortest entries in his notebook about exactly this, and it's barely a sentence long. Today: nothing at random.
screen: `WHY DID I PICK UP MY PHONE?` → `A DAY ON AUTOPILOT.` → `NOTHING AT RANDOM.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Let no act be done at random, Marcus writes in the second entry of book four, nor in any way other than by the principles of the craft. That's the whole entry. Second, the craft. The Stoics often spoke of living well as an art, a skill like carpentry or medicine. A good carpenter doesn't swing the hammer at random. Every cut is for the chair. Marcus is saying a life can be built the same way: each act for something. Third, why random acts hurt. Back in book two, Marcus listed the ways a soul does harm to itself, and one of them was letting any act or movement happen without an aim. A day made of random acts isn't neutral. It slowly teaches you that your life is something that happens to you. Fourth, the target. Seneca, writing about a century before Marcus, made a similar point with a sailor's picture: if you don't know which harbor you're making for, no wind is the right wind. Purpose doesn't have to be grand. It can be: I'm picking up my phone to answer my sister. I'm walking to the kitchen to drink water. I'm going to this meeting to listen well. Small purposes, named, turn drift into steering. Marcus isn't asking for a rigid schedule or a life with no rest. Rest on purpose counts. A walk with no destination, chosen, counts. What he's warning against is the act nobody chose, not even you.
screen: `LET NO ACT BE DONE AT RANDOM.` · `LIVING AS A CRAFT.` · `AIMLESS ACTS HARM THE SOUL.` · `NAME THE HARBOR.` · then, large: `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Choose one ordinary thing you'll do in the next hour: making tea, opening your email, walking to the car. Before you do it, name its purpose in a few words. I'm doing this to. Then picture doing it with that purpose in mind, start to finish, nothing extra. Notice how the same act feels when it's chosen. The bell holds the time.
Nothing at random. Marcus tells himself to let no act be done without an aim, as a craftsman makes every cut for the thing being built. Today's word.
Your line: on purpose. Do one thing on purpose today: before you start, say what it's for. Day five hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.2 by naming the purpose of an ordinary act, such as picking up the phone, before doing it.

fork.setup: you have twenty free minutes. you could scroll, or do something else. what fits Meditations 4.2?
options: scroll: it's free time, after all.
choose something, even rest, and name why.
fill it with any task to stay busy.
fork.reveal: Marcus asks only that no act be done at random. rest, chosen on purpose, passes his test.

original.note: Greek, 'at random, without aim': the word Marcus uses for the act he warns against in 4.2.

trapdoor: what it means: let every act, even rest, have a chosen aim.
what a scholar hears: the Stoics described virtue as a craft of living, so a random act is like a craftsman's careless cut.

notes: 4.2 paraphrased: let no act be done without a purpose (at random), nor otherwise than according to the perfect principles of art. Confirm.
2.16 lists among the ways the soul does violence to itself 'when it allows any act of its own and any movement to be without an aim'. Confirm.
Seneca, Letter 71.3: when a man does not know what harbor he is making for, no wind is the right wind. Confirm reference.
